Capital, Labour and Justice

Lecture 5: Redistribution

Dr David Chivers

Political Economy

What is inequality?

Inequality of what?

  • Income, wealth, consumption?
  • Within or between countries, groups or generations?
  • Relative or absolute?
  • Inequality of opportunity or outcome?
  • What measure e.g. Range, Gini coefficient or Top 1%?

Inequality

Wealth Inequality

Types of Income

  • Market income is the sum of…
  • all income received as earnings (wages, self-employment)
  • all income received from business owned by the household or from investments
  • Disposable income is the income that a family can spend
  • after paying taxes
  • after receiving any monetary transfers from the government (e.g. unemployment benefit and pensions)
  • Final Income: is the income that a family can spend
  • Subtract VAT paid.
  • Add the value of public services received.

Income Types

Types of Income

Countries that tend to reduce inequality do so via transfers rather than taxes:

  • Much of this justified for reasons other than redistributing income.
  • Social insurance, for example, is seen as redistributing from the lucky to the unlucky

Let’s look at the average Ginis within the EU in 2015

  • The Gini for market income is 0.46
  • The Gini for disposable income is 0.27
  • But taxes only achieve 0.04 of that redistribution
  • The remaining 0.15 driven is by transfers to households.
  • Note: this does not mean the EU has low tax rates, but instead it means that rich and poor pay similar shares of their incomes in taxes.
  • On the other hand, poorer households benefit proportionally from expenditures.

Measures of Inequality

Relative vs Absolute

  • Absolute inequality is a difference measure
  • Relative inequality is a ratio measure.
  • Let’s say two incomes £ 10,000 & £50,000 increase to £100,000 and £ 500,000, respectively
  • Absolute inequality gains as the difference moves from £40,000 to £ 400,000
  • Relative inequality remains at 1:5
  • Although absolute measures are important to pay attention to, most inequality measures are relative

Absolute Redistribution

Relative Redistribution

The Gini Coefficient

  • The most widely used measure of inequality is the Gini coefficient
  • The Gini coefficient is usually used to measure of income inequality,
  • However, but it can be used to measure the any forms of inequality (e.g. consumption or life expectancy)
  • The scale is from 0 to 1
  • The higher the value, the higher the level of inequality.
  • A value of 0 would mean perfect equality – everyone has the same income.
  • A value of 1 would mean perfect inequality – one person received all the income
  • The Gini coefficient is more sensitive around the middle of the distribution than at the top or bottom compared to other measures of inequality

Method 1: The Gap

  • The Gini coefficient is the expected absolute gap between people’s incomes relative to mean income
  • It is the gap we would expect if two people in the population met randomly
  • We can calculate it by taking the average gap between all pairs of people.
  • Specifically, we calculate it as the expected gap as a share of twice the mean income.
  • Twice the mean income is equal to perfect inequality. Why?
  • Suppose our economy is just two people and that their total income is £100.
  • Their average income is £50 (£100/2).
  • Under perfect inequality one person has £100 and the other £0
  • The gap between them will be £100… twice the mean income.

Method 2: Lorenz curve

  • If income is shared perfectly equally, the Lorenz curve would be a straight line
  • In the graph, the bottom 60% of the population earns 30% of the total income.
  • The Gini coefficient captures how far the Lorenz curve falls from the ‘line of equality’ by comparing the areas A and B

Value Judgements

  • Measures of inequality have value judgements implicitly built into them (Atkinson, 1970)
  • Which society has the greater levels of inequality?
  • Society 1: The rich are much richer than those in the middle, but poor people have incomes just below those with middle incomes
  • Society 2: The rich are just above those with middle incomes, but the poor are much poorer than those with middle incomes.
  • Your answer will depend on how you view these gaps in different parts of the distribution and how they compare in terms of the contribution they make to inequality.

Comparing Measures

Gini and Taxes

Redistribution

Pre-distribution

  • Before and after-tax income does not tell us the total reduction of inequality caused by redistribution
  • Taxes and benefits will have an effect on income before income has even been taxed
  • For example, you may decide not to work longer hours if you move to a higher tax bracket

This can make cross-country comparisons difficult

  • Public pensions are counted as redistribution, whereas private pensions are not.
  • Countries where public pensions are higher will likely see lower wages
  • But if there was no public pension scheme, we would expect those countries to receive higher wages.
  • CEOs bargain for more money, increasing pre-tax wage inequality (Piketty, Saez, and Stancheva, 2014)

Redistribution

Indirect taxes

  • Indirect taxes, such as consumption taxes (e.g. V.A.T) are not accounted for in redistribution measures
  • Poorer people, on average, spend a higher share of their income
  • Some say consumption taxes increase inequality as a result, but this is debateable (see next slide)

Government Spending:

  • Government cash transfers are not only way government spends money (e.g. education & public parks)
  • This type of government spending may benefit poorer people more but is difficult to measure

Two types of taxation:

  • Progressive taxation: When the direct effect of a tax or transfer policy (compared to what would happen in the absence of the policy) gives a reduction in inequality
  • Regressive taxation: If a policy’s direct effect causes a rise in inequality

Regressive or Progressive?

  • For an expenditure or transfer to be progressive, it must increase the incomes of poorer households by more than richer households, in relative terms.
  • This guarantees that it will reduce the Gini coefficient
  • Note that this policy might mean that in absolute terms, the richer households are receiving more

Is V.A.T. Regressive or Progressive?

  • V.A.T. is complex as it effects savings behaviour (Thomas, 2020)
  • Income that is saved will eventually be taxed by V.A.T. when it is consumed
  • We can remove savings behaviour by measuring it relative to current income or expenditure
  • It appears to be regressive if measured as a proportion of current income
  • It appears to be progressive if measured percentage of current expenditure

Wealth Taxes

  • There are two main disagreements among economist about annual wealth tax
  • Difficulty in implementation
  • Even if perfectly implemented, is it the right tool to achieve policy objective?
  • Imagine wealth of £100 gives capital income of £5 a year.
  • A 1% wealth tax is the same as a 20% capital income tax…£1
  • Imagine now wealth returned an excess capital income of £20 a year
  • A 1% wealth tax would return £1 but a capital income tax £4
  • There are strong arguments in favour of taxing excess returns over normal returns
  • Wealth taxes, however, do the opposite
  • If all income from work and all excess returns to capital were taxed (including inheritance tax) would there need to be a wealth tax?

Wealth Taxes

  • Three “principled rationales” for wealth taxes (IFS, 2021)

A wealth tax in order to tax savers

  • Some people are better at saving than others (e.g. have higher financial literacy)
  • “Use it of lose it”: tax normal returns more than excess as it rewards (and encourages) entrepreneurial activity (Guvenen et al., 2019)

A wealth tax when wealth has benefits beyond purchasing power

  • If wealth has benefits to the wealth-holder more than the consumption it can be derived from
  • Although this is debatable – perhaps they simply have not found the thing to spend it on.

A wealth tax when wealth has negative externalities

  • If wealth confers status, and status is a zero-sum game – it is relative position that matters
  • If wealth is harmful to others (although would have to be contingent on not spending the wealth)

Summary

  • We need to be specific about what type of inequality we mean
  • It is difficult to separate inequality measures from value judgements
  • Comparing redistribution across countries is hard because of pre-distribution
  • The extent to which wealth taxes are implementable or desirable is debateable
  • See Talis for reading list.
